whatTheyArgued: Truths of existence/faith cannot be directly communicated; the author uses indirect communication (pseudonyms, irony, Socratic maieutics) so the reader appropriates rather than receives them. Point of View for My Work as an Author sec. 2 (title as retrieved from search snippets): to lead a person to a position one must first find him where he is and begin there; the same text says to help someone one must first understand what he understands. Kierkegaard frames the aim as inwardness and the religious.

scholarship.supports: indirect communication, pseudonymity, appropriation vs verbal understanding, Point of View
scholarship.disputes: Scholars dispute whether Point of View is honest self-report or retrospective revisionism (journals suggest evolution).

scholarship.ref: Search results quoting Point of View section 2 heading and the 'understand what he understands' sentence (Hong translation excerpts; primary text not fetched by me)
scholarship.supports: the 'find him where he is' principle and the 'understand what he understands' sentence exist in the text
scholarship.disputes: our quotation with an ellipsis is a paraphrase-splice, not located verbatim

ourUse: socratic.js composes the reply to a decline as a plain question or reasons in a person/agent register, keeps the exact judgment on the audit record, never lets nothing-but-a-verdict be handed over.

bends.ours: compendium quotation: 'To help another, one must first understand what he understands... one must first and foremost meet him where he is.'
bends.theirs: Two separate passages (the 'understand what he understands' sentence, and the section-2 heading about finding him where he is) joined by an ellipsis into one sentence, in an uncredited translation; not verified as one sentence in the book.

bends.ours: Indirect communication used for honest, compliance-free explanation of a refusal.
bends.theirs: Kierkegaard's indirection is deliberately deceptive in service of a religious end ('deception into the truth' in Point of View); our code forbids exactly that ('dressing up manipulation as a question' is the one thing it must never do). The method is borrowed, the ethic is reversed.

bends.ours: Used as a customer-facing register for declines (a question for a person, reasons for an agent).
bends.theirs: Aimed at the reader's appropriation of existential/religious truth over a whole authorship, not at wording a single reply.

bends.ours: Canned per-KIND replies that end in a question.
bends.theirs: Socratic maieutics responds to what the particular person understands; a fixed template cannot meet them 'where he is'.

fix: compendium work: split the quotation into its two real sentences from one cited translation (Lowrie 1939 or Hong 1998) and drop the ellipsis; or paraphrase without quote marks.
socratic.js header: add 'Kierkegaard's indirection is also a method of deception toward truth; ours is not, and we refuse that half.'
